title: Mexican Senate Approves, with a Qualified Majority, Reform on Dual Nationality for Candidates
author: Andrea Becerril
content:
_This article by[Andrea
Becerril](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Andrea%20Becerril) originally
appeared in the [September 29, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/09/29/politica/senado-
aprueba-reforma-sobre-doble-nacionalidad-de-candidatos), Mexico's premier
left-wing daily newspaper._

**Mexico City**. The Senate today approved, with the backing of Morena and its
allies, a constitutional reform **requiring anyone seeking the presidency, a
state governorship, or the head of government of Mexico City to hold Mexican
nationality exclusively** ; candidates who also hold another nationality will
have to renounce it.

Morena and its allies reached exactly the **86 votes** required for the
qualified majority, bringing in alternates for four senators who could not
attend for various reasons. The full opposition voted against the measure,
along with the Green Party's (PVEM) Luis Armando Melgar, who had previously
said he would support it.

Over more than three hours of debate, Morena and its allies pushed back on the
opposition's recurring claims. The chairs of the Constitutional Affairs and
Legislative Studies committees, Oscar Cantón Zetina and Manuel Huerta Ladrón
de Guevara, rejected what they called the opposition's "lies," arguing the
measure is a matter of sovereignty and institutional loyalty, since whoever
aspires to lead the country must answer unambiguously to the interests of the
Mexican people above any other tie.

Presenting the committee's opinion, Morena Senator Saúl Monreal said the
reform does not seek to change the recognition of dual nationality that has
existed in Mexico since 1997: "The rule is clear — anyone seeking to head the
presidency, a governorship, or the head of government must be Mexican by birth
and not hold or acquire another nationality, for reasons of national
security."

Huerta Ladrón de Guevara likewise insisted the reform "is not aimed at anyone"
and does not change the right of millions of Mexicans to keep a second
nationality.

> Mexico recognizes dual nationality, it protects it, and this reform does not
> change that principle.
>
> Sen. Manuel Huerta Ladrón de Guevara

The opposition disagreed. PRI Senator Alejandro Moreno Cárdenas argued that
holding another nationality doesn't make any Mexican an enemy of the country,
but that the reform harms the rights of Mexicans born abroad. A PAN senator
accused Morena of treating migrants as second-class Mexicans: "They want
migrants' votes to stay in power and build artificial majorities, but they
don't want them to be elected." Movimiento Ciudadano's Luis Donaldo Colosio
Riojas said the measure amends the Constitution to regulate something already
covered by Article 32, and warned it could especially affect Mexicans born in
the United States by making their political rights depend on renouncing a
foreign nationality.

Two Morena senators offered personal testimony in response. **Ricardo
Sheffield Padilla** said he was born in the United States but renounced that
nationality at 18 — unlike his siblings, who "aren't interested in politics" —
and that he would vote for the reform without hesitation. **Gerardo Fernández
Noroña** accused the opposition of repeating the same falsehoods and pointed
to Latin American presidents, such as Colombia's, who hold dual nationality
and answer to Washington's interests.

At the moment of the vote, Movimiento Ciudadano's Alejandra Barrales demanded
that Senate President Higinio Martínez confirm that Senator Octavia Hernández
Farret — who was sworn in ahead of Karina Ruiz — had resigned from her job at
the Mexican consulate in San José. Hernández Farret clarified that she had
done so, stressing that she is a migrant living in the United States but
remains Mexican all the same.
